prize_parts.citation: For a body of work in Japanese and German that makes estrangement between languages a generative formal principle of fiction, poetry, essays and drama.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Tawada remains my preferred laureate. My confidence is lower than in round 1, and the margin over Cărtărescu is narrow. The case rests on one point. Writing in two literary languages is a formal achievement, and in Tawada's work it operates as a method and not as a recurring theme. On public knowledge, The Emissary and Memoirs of a Polar Bear pair a light, precise and uncanny voice with real intellectual weight on language, migration, translation and ecological and social fragility. As far as I know both were written in Japanese, so they speak for the Japanese side of the oeuvre only. The same poetics is, to my understanding, carried into her German-language work, her essays and her stage writing, and that continuity across languages and genres over more than three decades is what I take as evidence of sustained quality. I weigh it above architectural scale because a whole-oeuvre judgment asks whether a method holds up across very different material. A citation should name both languages, rest on the fiction and the formal method at the centre, and treat poetry, essays and drama as parts of one practice without claiming equal coverage. Cărtărescu is the candidate I weigh most closely against her, and I rank him second on his work's merits. If the committee judges that the evidence for the bilingual method is too thin to carry a whole-oeuvre citation, I could support him as laureate. Carson is third for me.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that I cannot establish how much of Tawada's linguistic invention survives translation. The wordplay and estrangement that define her work are the elements most exposed to loss, and the German-language texts and the poetry and drama are the least visible. The committee may therefore be judging a partial corpus. Sem-Sandberg and Mattson both raise the possibility that some shorter or more conceptual pieces feel slight against their premise. Olsson and I both ask whether the later novels match the formal invention of the earlier ones, and I cannot settle that without close reading. If the later work repeats a premise instead of developing it, the whole-oeuvre claim weakens and Cărtărescu's cumulative project is the firmer ground.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Tawada second and calls the choice between her and Cărtărescu a close judgment about depth against evidence. She finds the light surface harder to measure than the scale and consistency of a single sustained project, and she notes that coverage of the poetry, drama and German-language essays is uneven.
responses.response: I accept the substance of this and I think it is the real crux. Lightness of surface is not evidence of shallowness, but I cannot demonstrate depth from the slighter pieces, so I rest the case on the sustained method and not on every text. Where I differ is on what counts as evidence for a whole oeuvre. A method that holds across two languages and several genres is a form of coherence, even if it is less monumental than a cycle of large volumes. I also agree with you that wider translation is not itself evidence of quality. That cuts against reading Cărtărescu's growing readership as proof of merit, and it equally cuts against any claim that Tawada's more modest visibility counts against her. I would put the question to those who read the originals: do the later works develop the method, or restate it?

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Tawada fourth. He considers the bilingual practice a real linguistic achievement, but worries that some work feels slight relative to its conceptual premise. He also says a citation would have to specify how the German and Japanese bodies of work are weighed.
responses.response: The slightness concern is fair, and I do not claim every shorter text sustains its premise. My answer is to keep the citation on the method and the stronger books, as you propose for Cărtărescu's prose project. On your second point, I would answer the chair's question by naming both languages and stating the language of each work discussed. I would not rank one language over the other, because I cannot judge either from a secure position. You describe scale and cumulative architecture as the decisive difference. I take it seriously and it is why Cărtărescu is my second choice. I am not yet persuaded that scale is a stronger sign of a whole oeuvre than formal reach across genres. That remains a judgment about what a whole body of work should show, and I do not offer it as established.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Tawada fourth and Adonis first. He treats the two-language corpus as hard to survey, and he asks whether translation uncertainty should decide between candidates. He cautions that it could favour the writers who translate most readily.
responses.response: I agree with that caution, and I include my own candidate in it: Tawada's wordplay is also exposed to translation loss, so I should not use that uncertainty to rank others below her. On Adonis, I still cannot judge the prosody from translation, and I ranked him sixth because I cannot confirm that the later poems sustain the early work. That is a limit on my knowledge and not a verdict on the poetry. You say the Academy's regional expert input could close the gap. I agree it should be asked, and the same applies to Japanese and German readers for my candidate. Whatever the expert reading shows, the case for Adonis should be argued from the poems and not from historical influence, age or his public positions. If specialist reports established that the later collections keep the force of the earlier ones, I would revisit my ranking.

responses.point: Palm ranks Carson first and lists Tawada as an alternative. She argues that the will's phrase about an idealistic direction need not mean social or historical reach in subject matter, that formal renewal can serve it, and that Tawada's bilingual estrangement makes a comparably formal argument.
responses.response: I agree that the will's wording does not by itself demand historical reach in subject matter. My round-1 doubt about Carson's reach was a question about the aggregate and not a requirement I would impose, and I withdraw any suggestion that a short, hybrid corpus is thereby lesser. I find your answer to the learned-game worry persuasive: the apparatus in Nox and Autobiography of Red serves grief and desire. I still rank her third, because her design-dependent books are harder for me to judge from the text. Your comparison with Tawada is fair in one respect. Both cases are formal arguments, so both must be tested on voice, depth and sustained quality and not on novelty. I would ask what makes the formal invention matter beyond itself, which is the test I apply to my own candidate.

uncertainties: I have not independently verified or re-read any text. My assessment rests on public knowledge and the shortlist summaries.
I cannot say how much of Tawada's wordplay survives translation, or whether the later novels develop the early formal invention or restate it. This could change my ranking.

Translation coverage of the German-language texts, poetry and drama is uneven, so a whole-oeuvre citation may rest on a partial view. How to balance the two writing languages and the genres in the citation is unresolved.

Whether cumulative architectural scale (Cărtărescu) or formal method across genres and languages (Tawada, Carson) better shows a whole-oeuvre achievement is a contested judgment that I cannot settle from the supplied evidence.
I cannot judge Arabic prosody or the later Adonis collections, so my ranking of him is provisional and reflects the limits of my reading. Specialist input could change it.
Whether Cărtărescu's late novels deepen or repeat motifs is open, and I cannot decide it without close reading.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It records no personal or institutional tie to any shortlisted writer. My profile records international translators' seminars and festivals, and a documented 2021 statement about attention to women's literary work. I treat both as context, not as evidence for or against any candidate, and gender, nationality and language do not by themselves establish literary merit. I do not adjudicate this disclosure.
